sentences.text: The application is filed under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for an order of pre- arrest bail.

2. The petitioners are the accused 1 to 3 in Crime No.404/2024 of the Maradu Police Station,
Ernakulam, registered against them for allegedly committing the offences punishable under Sections 406 and 420 r/w Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
3. The essence of the prosecution case is that: the de facto complainant/second respondent is the Director of a company and is a native of Kollam.

In May 2022, the third accused (mother-in-law of the de facto complaint's brother) went to the office of the second respondent along with the first accused and sought for financial assistance to import curtain accessories and fabric from China.
The first accused made the second respondent believe that they would get a minimum profit of Rs.20,00,000/- on each container and that they would give him 22% of the profit, after deducting the TDS.
Believing the assurance made by the accused, the second respondent paid Rs.2.60/- crore to the accused.
Again, on 01.03.2023, the accused approached the second respondent and sought for an additional amount of Rs. 1.5/- crore on the assurance of the same profit.

Accordingly, the second respondent demanded the accused to enter into a partnership with him and open a bank account,
and the funds can be channelised through the bank account.
Believing the assurance made by the accused 1 and 2, the second respondent paid a further amount of Rs.1.60/- crore i.e. a total of Rs.4.10/- crore.
The accused 1 and 2 flourished in their business and led a luxurious life.
They informed the second respondent that they were facing severe difficulties in bringing containers to the Cochin Port Trust and, therefore, they had to unload the materials at the Chennai Port.
They said that 50% of the profit would have to be kept in the new account of the firm for the purpose of business.
When the second respondent asked the accused for the profit, the first accused said that he had gone to China and that he would pay the profit by September.
The accused only transferred some money to cover up their cheating.
Even though the second respondent made repeated demands, the accused did not pay the money.
It is then that the second respondent felt that the accused were cheating him.

The accused had issued seven post dated cheques for Rs.2.6/- crore,
towards the repayment of his amount, but the cheques got dishonured.
The accused have failed to pay the profit or return the capital to the de facto complainant.
Thus, the accused have committed the above offences.

4. Heard; Sri.M.R.Sarin, the learned counsel appearing for the petitioners, Smt.Seetha S., the learned Senior Public Prosecutor and Sri. Saiby Jose Kidangoor, the learned counsel appearing for the second respondent.

sentences.text: The learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the petitioners are totally innocent of the accusations levelled against them.
A reading of Annexure A4 complaint would clearly establish that the dispute between the parties is civil in nature.
The third petitioner and the second respondent are relatives.
The third petitioner's daughter is married to the second respondent's brother.
But, the marriage is strained and Annexure A8 proceeding is filed before the Family Court Ernakulam.
The present complaint is a counterblast and a retaliatory proceeding to Annexure A8.
The second respondent had paid Rs.4.10/- crore on 01.03.2023.
Subsequently, the second respondent and the first petitioner entered into Annexure A2 partnership deed, and Rs.1.5/- crore was adjusted towards the second respondent's capital in the firm.
Annexure A6 bank transactions clearly reveal that the petitioners have paid the agreed profit to the second respondent.
Annexure A2 partnership deed unambiguously provides for the settlement of all disputes between the parties through arbitration.
It is without taking recourse to the said alternative dispute mechanism, that the second respondent has approached the Investigating Officer and lodged the complaint, who refused to register the FIR.
Subsequently, the second respondent filed Annexure A4 complaint before the jurisdictional Magistrate and the complaint was forwarded to the Investigating Officer under Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C.
Then, Annexure A1 FIR was registered on 23.03.2024 i.e. after a year after the last transaction between the parties, which by itself proves the frivolity and falsity in the crime.
The petitioners have adhered to the terms and conditions of Annexure A2 partnership deed by importing materials from China and paying the agreed profits.
In fact, three containers have been imported as agreed by the parties.
Now that there is a strained relationship in the two families, the second respondent wants his capital back immediately.
Notwithstanding the above facts, the petitioners have issued seven post dated cheques to the second respondent towards repayment of his capital.

The above background undoubtedly establishes that the petitioners had no mens rea to cheat the second respondent right from the inception of him paying the capital, which is a pre- requisite to attract the alleged offence.
The investigation in the case is practically complete and recovery has been effected.
Therefore, the petitioners' custodial interrogation is not necessary.
The petitioners are ready to abide by any stringent condition that may be imposed by this Court.
Hence, the application may be allowed.
6. The learned Public Prosecutor opposed the application.
The Investigating Officer has filed a bail objection report, inter alia, contending that there are incriminating materials to substantiate the petitioners involvement in the crime.
The petitioners' custodial interrogation is necessary for the full and proper investigation of the crime.
Therefore, the application may be dismissed.
Nonetheless, the learned Public Prosecutor submitted that three containers were imported from China as per the agreement entered between the parties.
However, the petitioners have only fulfilled one-third of the contract and have not paid the agreed profit to the de facto complainant.
7. The learned counsel for the second respondent also seriously opposed the application.
He submitted that the petitioners had the mens rea to cheat the second respondent right from the time of making the false promise to the second respondent.

It is only because the petitioners' defaulted to keep up to their contractual obligations, that the first petitioner and the second respondent entered into Annexure A2 partnership deed to ensure that the petitioners paid the profit.
The petitioners have thoroughly cheated the second respondent and have not paid the assured profit or returned the capital as undertaken by them.

If the petitioners are granted an order of pre-arrest bail, there is Safarullah Kh vs State Of Kerala on 12 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/44804267/
3 every likelihood of them fleeing from justice because they are frequent travellers abroad.

8. The second respondent's case as per Annexure A4 complaint is that, the petitioners 1 and 3 had approached him for financial assistance on the assurance of paying him 22% of Rs.20,00,000/-on each container imported from China.
On the basis of the said promise, the second respondent paid Rs.4.10/- crore to the petitioners.

Subsequently, since the petitioners failed to keep up to their contractual obligations, the first petitioner and the second respondent entered into Annexure A2 partnership deed along with two others, wherein Rs.1.5/- crore is shown as the second respondent's capital.
9. It is undisputed that Annexure A2 deed was entered into between the parties, after the money was entrusted by the second respondent to the petitioners.
Clause 15 of Annexure A2 also proves that the parties have agreed that all their disputes would be settled through arbitration.

10. The petitioners contend that they have paid the profits as reflected in Annexure A6 bank statement, and the present complaint is only an offshoot of the matrimonial litigation between the third petitioner's daughter and the second respondent's brother.
It is only to harass and vex the petitioners and to pressurise them to yield to the second respondent's brother's unlawful demands that the present complaint is filed.
The second respondent, on the contrary, submits that the petitioners have failed to keep up to their contractual obligations.
Although the petitioners issued seven cheques to the second respondent towards the repayment of the profit, the cheques got dishonoured.
The Investigating Officer has stated that the petitioners have only imported three containers till date and have only fulfilled one-third of their contractual obligations.
The petitioners contend that they have paid the agreed profits, but the second respondent wants his capital back due to the strained relationship in the family.

Whether there was mens rea on the part of the petitioners to cheat the de-facto complainant as alleged in Annexure A4 complaint, is a matter to be investigated and ultimately decided at the time of trial.

11. In Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd. [(2006) 6 SCC 736], the Honourable Supreme Court has observed in the following lines:
"13. ....... Any effort to settle civil disputes and claims, which do not involve any criminal offence by applying pressure through criminal prosecution should be deprecated and discouraged".

No.9949/2023], after taking note of the fact that the crime was registered after six years from the alleged date of incident and the accused had joined the investigation, went on to observe that, even though custodial interrogation is one of the effective modes of investigation, it is equally true that just because custodial interrogation is not required that by itself may not be a ground to release an accused on anticipatory bail, if the offences are serious in nature.

sentences.text: However, a mere assertion on the part of the State while opposing a plea for anticipatory bail stating that custodial interrogation is necessary would not be sufficient.
The State has to show or indicate more than prima facie, why custodial interrogation of the accused is required for the purpose of investigation.

17. On an overall consideration of the facts, the rival submissions made across the Bar, and the materials placed on record, especially on comprehending the fact that it is after the money was entrusted by the second respondent to the petitioners on 01.03.2023, that he entered into Annexure A2 partnership deed with the first petitioner, and Annexure A4 complaint was filed only on 25.03.2024, and the second respondent himself has admitted that the petitioners have paid him some money, that the parties have agreed that their disputes will be settled through arbitration and finally there is a matrimonial dispute between the second respondent's brother and the third petitioner's daughter, I am prima facie convinced that the dispute between the parties seems to be civil in nature, though that is a matter to be ultimately decided after trial.

Therefore, I am satisfied and convinced that the petitioners have made out valid grounds to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court under Section 438 of the Code, particularly because the petitioners' have no criminal antecedents, they are willing to cooperate with the investigation, and their custodial interrogation is not necessary.
Hence, I am inclined to allow the application.
